Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Tama was forty-six years old, a man of Samoan descent living in a coastal American town, working as an auditor for a small firm. He had been widowed for eighteen months, ever since the night the tsunami came. That evening, he and his wife, Leilani, had been celebrating their anniversary on the beach, feeling happier than they had in months, lying on a blanket under the stars. The ocean had been calm, the air warm and still. Then, without warning, the water receded, leaving an unnatural silence that Tama would later describe as the most frightening thing he had ever heard. Before he could process what was happening, a wall of water had risen from the darkness and swept them both into chaos. He remembered the taste of salt and mud, the smell of seaweed and gasoline, and the way Leilani’s hand slipped from his grip. He survived by clinging to a piece of debris, but Leilani did not. For hours afterward, he floated in the inky black water, surrounded by silence broken only by distant screams. The event had ended, but in Tama’s mind, it had never stopped.

In the months that followed, Tama returned to his job as an auditor, a profession that required attention to detail but also a fixed routine. He found himself avoiding any new assignment that took him to an unfamiliar office building or neighborhood. He could not assess the danger in those places, he told himself, and that uncertainty felt too much like the seconds before the wave hit. At home, he began smoking more, lighting cigarettes during the moments when he caught himself starting to relax. Relaxing felt dangerous, as though any calm moment could be shattered by catastrophe. He refused invitations to dinner or social gatherings, not because he was sad, but because he could not bear to talk about the tsunami or its aftermath. When coworkers asked about his life, he changed the subject or excused himself.

The world had become a place where danger lurked in silence. At work, when the office fell unusually quiet—when phones stopped ringing and keyboards went silent—Tama’s heart would race, certain that something terrible was about to happen. The same feeling gripped him when a project took longer than expected. A delayed report or a late reply from a client made him assume the worst: that something bad was unfolding just beyond his awareness. At night, he struggled to sleep because waking up in the dark reminded him of the water and the terror. Even in his dreams, he could not escape. The memory of that night returned to him not as a story, but as a sensory assault. He could smell the salt and diesel fuel, taste the grit of sand and oil on his tongue, and feel the cold water against his skin. Some days, the memory was so extreme that it did not feel real, as though it had happened to someone else, and yet he knew it had happened to him. That contradiction left him feeling dead inside, hollowed out and incapable of joy.

His sense of helplessness had settled into a quiet conviction: he could not stop bad things from happening. He had believed, before that night, that he could protect those he loved. The tsunami had proved otherwise. Now, every decision was hedged by fear. He avoided unfamiliar places because he could not predict the danger. He avoided relaxation because it invited vulnerability. He avoided conversation because it demanded exposure. These strategies had once felt necessary, but they had cost him his friendships and his ability to feel connected to his adult children, who lived in a different state. They visited less and less often, discouraged by his withdrawn demeanor and his refusal to discuss the event that had changed everything.

What finally brought Tama to a therapist’s office was not a crisis, but a slow accumulation of loss. He had come to realize that his life had shrunk to the dimensions of his apartment, his office, and a few safe routes between them. He was tired of being afraid in silence. He was not sure he could change, but he was even more afraid of staying the same. What he hoped for, more than anything, was to feel something other than the cold numbness that had taken root inside him.
